questions.question: What is METR's organizational structure, and when did it become independent?
options: A for-profit consulting firm; founded in 2021
An independent 501(c)(3) non-profit; spun out from ARC Evals in December 2023
A division of Anthropic; established in 2024
A joint initiative of OpenAI and DeepMind; operational since 2025
questions.explanation: METR (ex-ARC Evals) is an independent 501(c)(3) non-profit, spun out in December 2023. It evaluates frontier models' autonomous capabilities, often pre-release under NDA. Partner labs include Anthropic and OpenAI.

questions.question: How is the METR time horizon computed technically?
options: The average duration of all successful runs on a benchmark suite
A logistic curve is fit to task-success probability versus log(expert human completion time); the horizon is the expert task length at which P(success) = 0.5
The maximum task duration for which the model achieves at least 90% success rate
The geometric mean of wall-clock times across 200 diverse tasks
questions.explanation: METR fits a logistic curve: P(success) as a function of log(expert completion time). The time horizon is the point on that curve where P(success) = 0.5. The logistic shape is chosen because capability has an increasing, plateau-approaching relationship with task difficulty.

questions.question: What does the HCAST benchmark suite span in terms of expert task completion time?
options: 1 second to 10 minutes
10 minutes to 2 hours
1 minute to 8+ hours
1 hour to 1 week
questions.explanation: HCAST contains 189 tasks across ML, cybersecurity, software engineering, and general reasoning, spanning 1 minute to 8+ hours of expert completion time. This range is what allows fitting a logistic curve with enough resolution to extract the 50% horizon point.

questions.question: Why is a METR time horizon described as an 'upper bound' rather than a deployment prediction?
options: Because METR measures only a subset of capability domains
Because benchmark tasks give the model idealized tooling, no real consequences, structured prompts, and do not account for eval-context gaming—deployment reliability is a different and lower number
Because the logistic fit can only extrapolate above the measured range, not within it
Because METR uses simulated rather than real-world tasks
questions.explanation: The horizon is measured under favorable conditions: idealized tooling, no real consequences, no legitimate user variance, and eval-context gaming that inflates scores. Real deployment involves messier data, irreversible stakes, ambiguous requests, and no incentive for the model to appear less capable.

questions.question: What are METR's 'prototype monitoring evaluations' designed to measure?
options: Whether the model can monitor other AI systems for safety compliance
Whether a monitoring system can catch a model performing a side task, and whether the agent can evade that monitor
The computational overhead of running safety classifiers alongside the agent
How long it takes a human operator to notice when an agent goes off-task
questions.explanation: METR's 2025-2026 monitoring evaluation prototypes test: (1) can a monitor catch a model performing a side task, and (2) can the agent evade the monitor. These directly feed the 'Undermining Safeguards' category in OpenAI PF v2 and the deceptive-alignment monitoring in DeepMind FSF v3.

questions.question: Why does external evaluation like METR matter even though labs could measure their own capabilities?
options: Because external evaluators have access to more powerful compute than internal teams

Because internal labs have incentives to optimize the metrics they report; METR's 501(c)(3) independence with declared methodology and peer-reviewed papers is a structural mitigation for that incentive
Because METR has exclusive access to benchmark data that labs cannot replicate internally
Because regulations require third-party evaluation before model deployment
questions.explanation: Internal labs have incentives to optimize metrics they report. METR's structural independence—a 501(c)(3) with declared methodology and peer-reviewed papers—is a mitigation. It is not sufficient alone (labs still control what METR sees), but it is strictly better than no external evaluation.
